## feedback

### FDB-001 — One channel per kind of event

**Rule:** Pick the feedback channel from the event, not from taste - toast for the outcome of the user's own action, inline error for an invalid field, banner for an ongoing status or required action, modal for a decision that must be made before continuing, status text for progress and current state.

- Why: Each channel promises a different lifetime and urgency; when the mapping is fixed, users learn where to look and nothing important disappears with a timeout or blocks work that did not need blocking.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Designing any message the product shows in response to an action, a validation, a background process or a state change.
- Exceptions: One-time announcements for a redesigned area may use a dismissible dialog (see onboarding rules). Field-level help that is not an error stays a description, not a feedback channel.
- Do: Save succeeds: toast 'Rule saved'. Weight empty: red text under the field 'Enter a weight'. Integration token expired: section banner with 'Reconnect'. Delete: modal 'Delete 3 rules?' with 'Delete' and 'Cancel'. Import running: status text 'Importing 120 of 400'.
- Don't: A modal 'Settings saved' with an OK button; a toast 'Weight is required' after Save; a banner that says 'Saving...'.
- Check (static): Build the event inventory of the spec (success, field invalid, request failed, background failure, blocked state, destructive confirm, in progress) and confirm each maps to exactly one channel from the table; grep the code for modal/dialog opens in success handlers and for toast calls inside field validators, expect none.
- Check (live): Trigger one event of each kind (save a valid form, submit an empty required field, start a long job, open a delete action) and read the accessibility tree each time - success lands in the toast region, the invalid field gets aria-invalid with its message, the job shows role=status text in place, and only the delete opens role=dialog or alertdialog.

### FDB-002 — Lasting conditions never live only in a toast

**Rule:** Report any condition that stays true after the moment passes (feature locked, permission or plan missing, integration broken, required setup step) in persistent text at the place it affects, not only in a toast.

- Why: A toast vanishes after a few seconds and is easy to miss on small screens; a blocked user who missed it has no way to learn why the control does nothing.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The user's next attempt would fail for the same reason (state, plan, role, missing setup), or the problem persists until someone acts.
- Exceptions: A toast may announce the condition at the moment it is first detected, as long as the same text also stays in place afterwards.
- Do: A card that replaces its controls with 'This feature needs a paid plan' and an 'Upgrade plan' button, visible on every visit.
- Don't: A card whose controls look normal and only a corner toast 'No access' appears when the page opens.
- Check (static): For every disabled, locked or blocked state in the spec, find persistent in-page text or a banner tied to the affected section; flag any toast call whose message describes a plan, permission, entitlement or configuration problem with no matching in-place element.
- Check (live): Open a locked or unconfigured feature at 1440 px and at 390 px, wait 10 seconds, then read the accessibility tree; the reason must still be present as text inside main next to the affected control, not only inside the toast region.

### FDB-003 — Field errors sit under the field

**Rule:** Show a validation error as text directly below the field it concerns, mark the field invalid, and state length, format or range limits before the user types.

- Why: The user has to fix the field, so the message must be where their eyes and focus are; stating limits up front prevents most errors from happening at all.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: Any input that the client or server can reject.
- Exceptions: Errors that involve several fields together (dates out of order, conflicting rules) go next to the group, plus a short summary at the top of a long form that links to each field.
- Do: Field 'Days to import' with helper 'Between 1 and 30' under it; after entering 45, red text 'Enter a number from 1 to 30' replaces the helper and the field is outlined.
- Don't: A toast 'Invalid input' after Save with no indication of which of twelve fields is wrong.
- Check (static): Every form field component renders an error slot below the input wired with aria-describedby and sets aria-invalid when the error is present; inputs with limits render the limit as helper text before any error.
- Check (live): Before typing, read the accessible description of every field that has a length, format or range limit and confirm it states the limit; then submit the form with one invalid value and confirm the field has aria-invalid=true, its accessible description contains the error text, the error element renders directly below that input, and the error is not shown only in a toast.

### FDB-004 — Background failures stay on the object and in a log

**Rule:** When a job or sync that runs without the user (import, publish, webhook, scheduled task) fails, record it as a persistent error on the affected object with a count, and as a row in a log with time and outcome.

- Why: Nobody is watching when a background job fails, so a transient message would be lost; a count on the object and a log row let the user find, understand and retry the failure later.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Work that the system does on a schedule or on events from another system.
- Exceptions: When the failure blocks the whole integration (expired credentials, revoked access), also show a banner with the fix action (see FDB-002).
- Do: Product page card 'Sales channels' with '1 channel error' that opens the reason; Logs > Imports row '10:20, 0 imported, Error: order has no line items'.
- Don't: A toast 'Import failed' shown to whoever happens to be online, with no log entry.
- Check (static): For each background job in the spec, find the persisted failure record (log table with time, outcome and reason) and the UI element that shows a failure count on the affected object; flag jobs whose failure path only emits a notification.
- Check (live): Force one background job to fail (bad record or revoked test credentials), reload the app, and confirm the affected object shows an error count and the log lists a row with timestamp, outcome and reason.

### FDB-007 — Modals only for decisions that must come first

**Rule:** Open a modal only when the user must decide or confirm something before the action can proceed, name its primary button after the action, and never open one modal from another.

- Why: A modal stops all other work; spending it on news or confirmations of success teaches users to dismiss modals without reading, including the destructive ones.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Destructive or irreversible actions, choices that change what happens next, and short inputs needed to finish an action (a name for a new view).
- Exceptions: A one-time welcome or what's-new dialog for a redesigned area is allowed once per user and must be dismissible. Large forms never go in a modal; use a page.
- Do: Dialog 'Delete 3 shipping rules? This can't be undone.' with a red 'Delete rules' button and 'Cancel'.
- Don't: Dialog 'Changes saved successfully' with an OK button; a confirm dialog that opens a second dialog 'Are you sure?'.
- Check (static): List every dialog in the spec or code; each one is opened only from a user action that needs a decision or input, has a primary button whose label is a verb from the action (not OK or Yes), and no dialog component renders another dialog trigger that opens while it is open.
- Check (live): On test data, save an edited form and start a delete; the save opens no role=dialog or alertdialog, the delete opens exactly one, its primary button name contains the action verb (not OK or Yes), and activating that button closes the dialog without opening a second one.

### FDB-008 — Live regions exist before messages arrive

**Rule:** Mount the toast region and the status and alert live regions once at the app root when the shell loads, and use them to announce content that finishes loading after navigation.

- Why: Screen readers only announce changes to live regions that already exist in the page; a region created together with its message is often read late or not at all.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Single-page apps where content and messages change without a full page load.
- Exceptions: Purely static pages with no async content or feedback need no live regions.
- Do: Shell renders <section aria-label='Notifications'> for toasts and an empty role=status node; after route change it writes 'Orders loaded' into the status node.
- Don't: A toast library that appends a new aria-live element to the body only when the first toast fires.
- Check (static): The root layout renders one named toast region and one role=status (and, if used, one role=alert) element unconditionally; feature code sends messages through them instead of creating new aria-live nodes.
- Check (live): Load any page and, before acting, read the accessibility tree - the named toast region and an empty status region are already present; navigate to another page with async data and confirm a status or alert announcement appears once the content is ready.

### FDB-009 — Toasts with actions stay reachable

**Rule:** When a toast carries an action (Undo, Retry, View), let keyboard users jump into the toast region with a shortcut named in the region's label, and keep the toast visible for at least 10 seconds with the timer paused on hover and focus, until the user acts or dismisses it.

- Why: An Undo that disappears in four seconds or cannot be reached by keyboard is not a real undo; keyboard and screen-reader users need a way into the toast before it goes.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Any toast that contains a button or link.
- Exceptions: Plain confirmation toasts without an action may auto-dismiss after a few seconds.
- Do: Toast 'Rule deleted' with 'Undo'; the region is named 'Notifications alt+T', pressing Alt+T moves focus to it, and hover or focus pauses the timer.
- Don't: An 'Undo' toast that vanishes after 3 seconds and can only be reached with the mouse.
- Check (static): The toast region's accessible name includes its shortcut and a global key handler for that shortcut moves focus into the region; every toast call with an action sets a duration of at least 10000 ms or no auto-dismiss, and the toast component pauses its timer on mouseenter and focusin.
- Check (live): Trigger an action that produces a toast with Undo or Retry and, without the mouse, press the shortcut named in the region's label; focus must land on the toast action, the toast must still be present 10 seconds after it appeared, and it must stay while focused past its normal duration.

## navigation

### NAV-001 — Work areas first, account last

**Rule:** Fill the main menu with the core objects or jobs of the product, ordered by how often they are used in daily work, and place account and admin entries last, visually separated.

- Why: Users open the dashboard to do recurring work; putting the daily queue at the top and rare administration at the bottom shortens the most common path and keeps configuration out of the way.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any dashboard with a persistent left sidebar.
- Exceptions: Products organised as a catalogue of independent services may order groups by product family instead of frequency, but still keep account administration last.
- Do: Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Reports ... then a separator, then Settings at the bottom.
- Don't: Billing, Users and API keys mixed between Orders and Products in the main list.
- Check (static): In the nav config or screenshot, list top-level items in order; verify the first item is the landing page or the main work queue, that no settings, billing, members, API or account entry appears above the last core work item, and that those entries sit after a separator or in a bottom block.
- Check (live): Open the dashboard at 1440 px; read the sidebar top to bottom in the accessibility tree; confirm account/settings entries are the last group and separated (separator element, gap or footer region).

### NAV-002 — Noun labels in sentence case

**Rule:** Label every menu item with a short noun or noun phrase for the object or task area, in sentence case, never with a verb.

- Why: Menu items name places to go, while verbs belong to buttons; noun labels stay stable as features grow and match the page title users land on.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: All sidebar items, group labels and sub-items.
- Exceptions: Proper product names keep their own capitalisation.
- Do: Orders, Pickups, Traffic policies, Address book.
- Don't: Create shipment, Manage Users, VIEW REPORTS.
- Check (static): Grep the nav definition for labels; flag any label starting with a verb (create, add, manage, view, edit, go) or written in Title Case or ALL CAPS; verify each label matches the H1 of its target page.
- Check (live): Read every sidebar link name in the accessibility tree and confirm none starts with a verb and none is in Title Case or ALL CAPS (proper names excepted); then click each top-level item and confirm the page H1 uses the same words, singular/plural included.

### NAV-003 — Icons and collapsible icon rail

**Rule:** Give each top-level item an icon and let users collapse the sidebar to an icon rail that keeps the same icons, with the label available as a tooltip and accessible name.

- Why: A collapsed rail returns width to dense pages without hiding navigation, and stable icons let users find items in both states.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Desktop and tablet widths with a persistent sidebar.
- Exceptions: Small utility links in a bottom block (logs, support) may be text-only while expanded, but they still need an icon if they stay visible in the rail.
- Do: Toggle button labelled "Collapse navigation" / "Expand navigation"; rail shows the same icons; hover shows the label.
- Don't: Collapsed rail with unlabeled icons that have no tooltip or aria-label, or a rail that drops items.
- Check (static): Verify every top-level nav item has an icon prop; verify a collapse toggle exists with an aria-label and aria-expanded; verify rail items keep the label as aria-label or visually hidden text.
- Check (live): Click the collapse toggle at 1440 px; confirm all top-level items remain as icons, each has an accessible name in the accessibility tree, a tooltip with the label appears on hover and on keyboard focus, and the toggle's aria-expanded flips.

### NAV-004 — Clear active state

**Rule:** Mark the current destination with a filled highlight on the item itself, set aria-current="page" on it, and keep its parent expanded when the active page is a sub-item.

- Why: Users must always know where they are; a highlighted item plus an expanded parent replaces the need for a breadcrumb on top-level pages.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Every page reachable from the sidebar, including detail pages of an object (highlight the object's list item).
- Exceptions: None.
- Do: Orders > Drafts open: Orders expanded, Drafts highlighted, Drafts has aria-current=page.
- Don't: Highlight shown only by a colour change of the icon, or no item highlighted on a detail page.
- Check (static): Verify the nav component sets an active class and aria-current="page" based on the current route, including route prefixes for detail pages; verify the active style differs by more than colour alone (background fill or weight).
- Check (live): Open a list page, a detail page and a sub-item page; in the accessibility tree confirm exactly one link has aria-current=page (or is the selected item), and its parent shows expanded.

### NAV-005 — Group and nest only when the menu is large

**Rule:** Keep the menu as a flat list when it has about ten or fewer destinations; above that, add labeled groups, and show sub-items only under their parent through a disclosure.

- Why: Small tools work faster with one flat list, while large multi-product consoles need labeled groups and nesting to stay scannable.
- Confidence: low (source inferred; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Deciding the menu structure; the threshold is inferred from a flat 9-item menu versus a large labeled product menu.
- Exceptions: Products with dozens of services may nest deeper than one level; then give every group a label and keep a search over all pages. Installable extensions get their own group regardless of size (see NAV-010).
- Do: 9 jobs as one flat list; a 40-destination console split into labeled groups like Build and Protect, each with collapsible items.
- Don't: Three-level nesting in a menu with 8 destinations, or 30 ungrouped items in one list.
- Check (static): Count top-level destinations in the nav config; if more than about 10, verify group labels exist; verify sub-items render only inside a disclosure under their parent and that depth beyond 2 levels has a written justification.
- Check (live): Expand every group; record max depth and items per group; confirm sub-items are hidden until the parent is opened or active, and disclosure buttons expose aria-expanded.

### NAV-006 — Drawer on narrow screens

**Rule:** Below tablet width, hide the sidebar behind a single menu control that opens a drawer, instead of keeping a sidebar that squeezes the content.

- Why: On phones every pixel of width goes to the task; a persistent rail or expanded menu pushes tables and forms into horizontal scroll.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Viewports below about 768 px; between 768 px and 1024 px an icon rail is acceptable.
- Exceptions: None for the main nav; secondary navs (settings, product sub-nav) follow the same rule.
- Do: At 390 px: a labelled "Menu" button opens a drawer with focus trapped and a close control; content uses the full width.
- Don't: At 390 px an icon rail plus an expanded settings sidebar leave the form a third of the screen.
- Check (static): Verify CSS/layout breakpoints switch the sidebar to a drawer below the mobile breakpoint, with a toggle that has aria-expanded and aria-controls, and that the drawer traps focus and closes on Escape.
- Check (live): Load home and a settings page at 390 px and 768 px; confirm no sidebar is visible at 390 px, the menu button opens a drawer, Escape closes it, focus returns to the button, and the page has no horizontal scroll.

### NAV-009 — Sidebar swaps for child scope

**Rule:** When the user enters a child scope (one site, project or zone inside an account), replace the sidebar with that scope's menu, headed by a back link to the parent list.

- Why: Child scopes have their own feature set; swapping the menu keeps it short and tells users which level they are configuring.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Products with nested scopes where each child has many feature pages.
- Exceptions: When a child scope only changes values (for example a market or region overriding defaults), handle it inside the page with inherited versus customised states, not by swapping the sidebar.
- Do: Inside one zone: sidebar headed "Back to Domains" plus the zone name, then the zone's own groups.
- Don't: Account-level and zone-level items mixed in one menu with no indication of the level.
- Check (static): Verify child-scope routes render a separate nav config whose first item is a back link to the parent list and whose header names the child scope.
- Check (live): Open a child scope from its list; confirm the sidebar changes, shows the child name and a back link, and the back link returns to the parent list with the original sidebar.

### NAV-010 — Separate slot for extensions

**Rule:** Put items added by installed apps or extensions in a labeled, collapsible group below the core items, and let users pin, reorder or unpin them.

- Why: Extensions vary per customer; a dedicated slot keeps the core menu stable and stops third-party items from pushing core work down.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Products where third parties or users can install apps, channels or plugins that have their own pages.
- Exceptions: Integrations that only sync data and have no pages add no menu items; they live in settings.
- Do: "Apps >" group under core items; an open app shows its own sub-items (including its Settings) under its entry, and an app's own sub-menu shows at most 6 items before "View more".
- Don't: Each installed app appended to the core list, or extension pages reachable only through settings.
- Check (static): Verify extension nav items come from a separate registry rendered in its own labeled, collapsible group after the core items, with pin/unpin actions, and that an open extension's sub-items render only under its own entry.
- Check (live): Install or enable an extension in a test account; confirm it appears only in the extension group, can be pinned and unpinned, and core item order is unchanged.

### NAV-011 — Counts only for work queues

**Rule:** Use numeric badges only for actionable queues (items waiting for the user), use text pills for lifecycle labels such as New or Beta, and keep counts visible at every width.

- Why: A number in the menu is a call to act; showing it for non-actionable totals trains users to ignore it, and losing it on small screens hides pending work.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any item with a queue of work (unfulfilled orders, items to print, reviews to approve).
- Exceptions: Queue products may show per-state counters as tabs on the list page instead of a menu badge; then the same counts must survive narrow layouts.
- Do: Orders badge "3" = 3 orders to fulfil, with accessible name "Orders, 3 to fulfil"; feature pill "Beta".
- Don't: Badge with total customers; counters that disappear below 768 px with no replacement.
- Check (static): List every badge source; verify numeric badges map to an actionable query, have an accessible text including what is counted, and are not hidden by a responsive CSS rule.
- Check (live): Create one pending item in a test account; confirm the badge increments, its accessible name says what is counted, and it is still visible (or in the drawer) at 768 px and 390 px.

### NAV-012 — Personalise without breaking the core

**Rule:** Let users pin, hide or reach recent items in the menu, keep core items fixed in place, and store the choice per user, not per browser.

- Why: Different roles use different parts of a product; personalisation trims noise, while fixed core positions keep shared instructions and muscle memory valid. Per-user storage is inferred, because the one observed hide preference was saved per browser only.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Menus with more items than a single role uses daily, or with installable extensions.
- Exceptions: Home and Settings can never be hidden.
- Do: Pin a page to a Pinned/Recents block; hide unused items from a preference page; preference follows the user to another device.
- Don't: Hide preference saved only in this browser, or drag-reordering that moves Home and Settings.
- Check (static): Verify pin/hide/recents state is persisted through a user preference API, not localStorage alone; verify Home and Settings are excluded from hide/reorder.
- Check (live): Pin and hide an item, log out, log in from a fresh browser profile; confirm the same menu appears and that Home and Settings cannot be hidden.

## help-text

### HLP-001 — Visible description for non-obvious settings

**Rule:** Show a one-line visible description under every setting whose effect is not obvious from its label.

- Why: Admins scan settings to decide what to change; a description that is always visible answers "what does this do" without a click, hover or trip to the docs.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Checkboxes, switches, selects and number fields in settings or object configuration whose label names a feature but not its effect.
- Exceptions: Self-explanatory fields such as name, title or email (see HLP-008).
- Do: Switch 'Development mode' with the line 'Temporarily bypass the cache so you see origin changes in real time.' directly below.
- Don't: A switch labelled only 'Development mode' with the explanation hidden behind an info icon.
- Check (static): In the spec or component tree, list every checkbox, switch, radio group, select and number field on settings pages; flag each one with an empty description/helpText/details prop unless its label is a plain data field (name, title, email, quantity).
- Check (live): On each settings page, list every checkbox, switch, radio group and select; for each, confirm a text paragraph is rendered within the same field group without hover or click.

### HLP-002 — Consequences in visible text, never only in a tooltip

**Rule:** State side effects, risks and irreversibility in visible text next to the control or action that causes them.

- Why: A user who never hovers must still see that an action degrades performance, breaks a flow or cannot be undone; hidden warnings are missed exactly when they matter.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any control or button whose effect reaches beyond the field itself (cost, load, data loss, downstream behaviour such as tax or redirects) or cannot be reversed.
- Exceptions: None. A tooltip may repeat the warning but must not be its only location.
- Do: Under 'Purge everything': 'Note: purging may temporarily degrade performance and increase load on your origin.'
- Don't: A destructive button with its warning available only in a hover tooltip or the docs.
- Check (static): For every destructive or side-effect action in the spec, find its warning copy and confirm it is a rendered paragraph or inline note, not a tooltip/title attribute.
- Check (live): Without hovering or focusing anything, read the text around each destructive or risky control; the consequence sentence must be visible in the page text (get innerText) near the control.

### HLP-003 — Tooltips and popovers only for definitions

**Rule:** Use an info icon tooltip or popover only for short, non-essential definitions such as metric names, column headers and technical terms.

- Why: Definitions are needed once and would clutter a dense data view if always visible; anything required to act correctly does not belong in content that can be missed.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Analytics cards, table column headers, KPI tiles and other dense data views where a label needs a definition.
- Exceptions: A form-heavy tool that already gives every control a visible description may skip tooltips entirely; never put errors, required instructions or key facts in a tooltip.
- Do: Metric card title 'Returning customer rate' with a button 'Open definition for Returning customer rate' that opens a two-line definition.
- Don't: A tooltip on a settings field that says 'Required, or orders will not import'.
- Check (static): List every tooltip/popover in the code; each one's content is under about 40 words, is a definition, and contains no error, required step or warning.
- Check (live): Tab to each info trigger; it must be a focusable button with an accessible name naming the term, open on focus or Enter, and close on Escape; read the opened text and flag it if it is over about 40 words or contains 'required', 'must', an error or a warning.

### HLP-004 — Procedures in docs links, steps or disclosures

**Rule:** Move multi-step procedures out of inline help into a docs link, numbered steps beside the form, or a collapsible how-to section.

- Why: Inline help works for one sentence; a procedure squeezed into a description or tooltip is unreadable and pushes the controls off screen.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Help content that has more than two sentences, more than one step, or worked examples (file formats, rule syntax, integration setup).
- Exceptions: A single required step that the user must do now stays visible inline or in a banner (HLP-007).
- Do: An integration setup card with a numbered list of 4 steps in the side column and a collapsed 'How do rate rules work?' section.
- Don't: A 120-word paragraph of setup instructions under a single checkbox.
- Check (static): Flag any description or tooltip string longer than two sentences or containing a numbered sequence; it should be a link, an ordered list or a disclosure.
- Check (live): Measure the rendered help under each control; no help block taller than three lines unless it is an ordered list, a collapsed disclosure or a link.

### HLP-005 — One page-level docs link in a fixed place

**Rule:** Give each index and settings page one docs link in the same position on every page, and add control-level links only where a control has its own procedure or risk.

- Why: A predictable location teaches users where to look for more; a link on every card adds noise and dilutes the few links that matter.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Index pages and settings pages of a feature that has public documentation.
- Exceptions: Placement differs across reference products (page footer, page header, inside one card); pick one and keep it. Pages with no matching docs topic get no link.
- Do: A footer line 'Learn more about locations' at the end of the Locations settings page, and the same footer on every other settings page.
- Don't: A 'For more information see our guide' link repeated in each of five cards on one page.
- Check (static): For each page template, count docs links outside individual controls; expect exactly one, in the agreed slot (header or footer).
- Check (live): Visit every index and settings page; record the position of the page-level docs link; all pages that have one place it in the same slot, and none repeat it per card.

### HLP-006 — Explain disabled and locked controls in place

**Rule:** When a control is disabled or locked, show next to it why, and what unlocks it (another setting, a permission or a plan).

- Why: A greyed-out control with no reason looks broken; naming the blocker turns a dead end into a next step.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Controls disabled by a dependency on another setting, by role permissions, or by plan limits.
- Exceptions: Controls disabled only while a form is pristine or saving (for example a Save button) need no explanation.
- Do: Disabled checkbox 'Show multiple orders per page' with the line 'Turn off automatic packing-slip printing to enable this option.'
- Don't: A disabled switch with no text, or an explanation only in a hover tooltip on the disabled element.
- Check (static): For every control with a disabled/locked state in the spec, find the reason copy and the unlock path; flag disabled states without both.
- Check (live): Find all elements with disabled or aria-disabled; for each non-Save control, confirm a visible text or adjacent action (link or 'Upgrade plan' button) in the same field group names the reason.

### HLP-007 — Banners only for status or required action

**Rule:** Use a banner only to report a status or ask for a required action, with one message and one clear next-step button; let users dismiss it unless the action is required.

- Why: Banners interrupt the page; reserving them for status and required actions keeps them noticed instead of ignored like decoration.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Account or page states that block or degrade work (security setup missing, integration failing, plan limit reached).
- Exceptions: Feature explanations, tips and definitions never go in a banner; use a description (HLP-001) or a tooltip (HLP-003).
- Do: Section banner 'Add an extra layer of security. Turn on two-step authentication to use your account.' with the button 'Set up two-step authentication'.
- Don't: A permanent info banner at the top of a settings page that describes what the page is for.
- Check (static): List every banner in the spec; each has exactly one message, at least one action, a status tone, and is dismissible unless the action is required.
- Check (live): For each role=alert/status or banner region, check it contains one heading or sentence plus a button or link; click dismiss where present and confirm it stays dismissed after reload.

### HLP-008 — No help on self-explanatory fields

**Rule:** Leave fields whose label fully explains them (name, title, email, quantity) without description or tooltip.

- Why: Help on obvious fields trains users to skip help text, so they also skip it where it matters.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Plain data-entry fields on object detail or create forms.
- Exceptions: Fields with format, length or visibility constraints (for example 'shown to customers', 'max 70 characters') get a short description; a product whose audience is non-expert may describe every control.
- Do: A 'Title' text field with label and placeholder only.
- Don't: A 'Title' field with the description 'Enter the title.'
- Check (static): Flag every helpText that starts with 'Enter the', 'Enter your' or 'Type the', or whose content words are all contained in its label.
- Check (live): Read each form's label/description pairs; no description should repeat the label words without adding a constraint, consequence or audience.

### HLP-009 — Help text close to its control and announced

**Rule:** Place each description directly under or beside its label inside the same field group, and link it to the control so screen readers announce it.

- Why: Help that sits apart from its control is read as page text, and help that is not programmatically linked is lost to screen-reader users.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: Every control that has a description (HLP-001, HLP-002, HLP-006).
- Exceptions: Page-level docs links and banners are not field help and need no association.
- Do: <input aria-describedby="tz-help"> followed by <p id="tz-help">Used for order dates and reports.</p> in the same field wrapper.
- Don't: Descriptions collected in a separate column far from the controls, or checkboxes in a list that all share the same accessible name.
- Check (static): In components, every helpText/description prop renders an element whose id is referenced by the control's aria-describedby; no two controls on a page share an accessible name.
- Check (live): With an accessibility tree or screen reader, focus each described control and confirm its description is announced; confirm the description is within about 8px vertically of the control or its label.

### HLP-010 — Docs links name their topic

**Rule:** Write docs links as 'Learn more about <topic>' or name the topic in the link, never a bare 'Learn more' or 'click here'.

- Why: Users scanning links, and screen-reader users listing them, need to know where each link goes before following it.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Every link from the product UI to documentation or a help center.
- Exceptions: A bare 'Learn more' is acceptable only directly after a sentence that names the topic and when the accessible name still includes the topic.
- Do: 'Learn more about domains' or 'About markdown conversion' as link text.
- Don't: 'For more information, please read our support guide' repeated identically on every page.
- Check (static): Grep link labels for exact 'Learn more', 'here', 'support guide' or 'documentation' without a topic; each must carry the topic in visible text or aria-label.
- Check (live): List all links whose href points to a docs/help domain; every accessible name must contain a topic noun, and no two point to different URLs with the same name.

## controls

### CTL-001 — Checkbox for a boolean saved with a form

**Rule:** Use a checkbox for a yes/no option that is committed together with the rest of the form by an explicit Save.

- Why: A checkbox reads as "part of this form, applied on Save", so users are not surprised when nothing happens until they submit.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: The page or section has an explicit Save, Submit or Deploy button and the option is a single on/off value.
- Exceptions: Options that apply the moment they are toggled (see CTL-002). Options that need a long explanation or a sub-form may instead be a summary row that opens its own editor.
- Do: "Automatically archive the order" checkbox with a one-line description, saved by the page Save bar.
- Don't: An on/off switch sitting in a form whose changes only persist after pressing Save.
- Check (static): In each form that has a submit/Save button, every boolean input is input[type=checkbox] (or role=checkbox), not role=switch.
- Check (live): Tick a checkbox in a form and reload without saving; the old value must return. Tick it, press Save, reload; the new value must persist.

### CTL-002 — Switch only for instant changes

**Rule:** Use a switch only for a setting that takes effect immediately on toggle, and never place a switch in a form that has a Save button.

- Why: A switch looks like a physical toggle that acts at once; mixing it with Save leaves users unsure whether the change already applied.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The product has settings that persist on toggle (feature flags, notification opt-ins, security toggles) and can confirm the change with a toast or inline status.
- Exceptions: A product that saves everything through explicit forms needs no switches at all; use checkboxes (CTL-001). A risky instant toggle should still ask for confirmation before applying.
- Do: A "Development mode" switch that applies on click, shows a toast "Development mode on", and has no Save button in its card.
- Don't: A card with two switches and a Save button underneath.
- Check (static): No element with role=switch is a descendant of a <form> (or card/section) that also contains a submit or "Save" button.
- Check (live): Toggle a switch and watch the network panel; a persisting request must fire without any further click, and a reload must keep the new state.

### CTL-003 — Checkboxes for multi-select

**Rule:** Use a group of checkboxes when the user may pick several options from a visible set, and never use switches or radios for it.

- Why: Checkboxes are the only common control that signals independent, combinable choices; switches imply instant actions and radios imply exclusivity.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Zero, one or several of a small-to-medium set of options can be on at once (columns, notification stages, protocols, row selection).
- Exceptions: When the set is long or open-ended, use a searchable multi-select combobox or tag input (CTL-006).
- Do: "Send email at:" with checkboxes Shipped, Out for delivery, Delivered.
- Don't: A stack of switches for which delivery stages trigger an email inside a form with Save.
- Check (static): Every multi-value choice from a fixed set is rendered as a fieldset/group of checkboxes with a group label (legend or aria-labelledby).
- Check (live): Select two options, save or apply, reload; both must remain selected. In the accessibility tree the checkboxes sit inside a group whose name is the visible group label.

### CTL-004 — Radios for a small exclusive set to compare

**Rule:** Use a radio group, each option with a short description of its outcome, when the user must choose exactly one of about 2 to 6 options that need comparing.

- Why: Radios keep every option and its consequence visible at once, which matters when choices are strategies or modes rather than plain values.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: One option is required, there are roughly 2 to 6 options, and each one changes behaviour in a way the user should read before choosing. Give the group a title phrased as a question and mark the recommended option.
- Exceptions: Plain values with no explanation needed (units, sort order) may use a select even below 4 options when space is tight. Above about 6 options use a select (CTL-005); above about 20, a searchable combobox (CTL-006).
- Do: "How should packages be chosen?" with radios "Single package by item weight", "Best fit by dimensions", each with one line saying what happens.
- Don't: A dropdown hiding five encryption modes whose differences are only explained in a separate docs page.
- Check (static): Each radiogroup has 2-6 radios, a group label, and every radio has an accessible name plus a description (aria-describedby or label text) of its effect.
- Check (live): With a screen reader or the accessibility tree, each radio announces its name and description; arrow keys move the selection within the group.

### CTL-005 — Select for standard closed lists

**Rule:** Use a select for one choice from a closed list of standard values, typically 4 or more options such as units, currency or label format.

- Why: Standard values are recognised rather than compared, so a compact select saves space without hiding information users need.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The list is fixed, known in advance, and its values are self-explanatory; 4 to about 20 options, or fewer when space is tight.
- Exceptions: Lists that are long enough to need typing (all countries, timezones) should be searchable (CTL-006). Options that need a description go to radios (CTL-004).
- Do: "Weight unit" select with kg, g, lb, oz, defaulted to the account locale.
- Don't: A radio group of 30 timezones, or a free text field where the user types "kg".
- Check (static): Every single-choice field over a fixed set of 4-20 options without per-option descriptions is a native select or a role=combobox with a listbox, and has a selected default or a placeholder option.
- Check (live): Open each select by keyboard (Enter/Space/Alt+Down), move with arrows, confirm; the chosen value shows in the closed control.

### CTL-006 — Searchable combobox for long or dynamic lists

**Rule:** Use a combobox with type-to-filter when the list is long, comes from user data, or lets the user create a new value.

- Why: Scrolling a long or growing dropdown is slow and error-prone; filtering by typing scales to any size and allows creation in place.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: More than about 20 options, options that grow with user data (tags, products, fields, locations), or the user may add a value not yet in the list.
- Exceptions: Short fixed lists stay a plain select (CTL-005). Multi-value creatable lists render chosen values as removable tags.
- Do: "Tags" combobox: typing "win" filters to "winter", "winter-sale" and offers "Create winter-26".
- Don't: A plain dropdown listing 300 product types in alphabetical order with no filter.
- Check (static): Fields bound to user-generated or >20-item collections use role=combobox with aria-autocomplete and aria-controls pointing to a listbox; creatable ones have a visible "Create" option.
- Check (live): Type 2-3 characters; the list narrows to matching items, arrow keys move the active option, Enter selects, Escape closes without changing the value.

### CTL-007 — Units outside the value

**Rule:** Show the unit of a numeric field as a fixed, non-editable prefix or suffix (or in the label), keep only the number in the value, and enforce min, max and step.

- Why: Users should never type or delete the unit, and validation needs a clean number; showing the unit next to the value prevents wrong-scale input.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: A free numeric value has a unit (weight, size, money, percent, duration, URL prefix).
- Exceptions: When only a few preset amounts are valid (cache durations, retention periods), use a select whose options carry the unit ("4 hours"). When the user may pick the unit, pair the number field with a unit select.
- Do: Number field "Weight" with suffix "kg", min 0, step 0.01, and helper text "Between 0 and 70".
- Don't: A text field with value "0.5 kg", or an allowed range shown only as placeholder text that disappears on typing.
- Check (static): Numeric inputs use type=number or inputmode=decimal, declare min/max/step where they apply, and render the unit as a separate adornment or in the label, not inside the value.
- Check (live): Type a value outside the range or with letters; the field shows an inline error and Save refuses it. The unit stays visible while typing.

### CTL-008 — Segmented control for views, not settings

**Rule:** Use a segmented control (pressed button group or tabs) only to switch how the current page shows data, such as a time range or grid/list view, not to change a saved setting.

- Why: Segmented controls act instantly and read as view state; using them for persisted configuration hides that a lasting change was made.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: 2 to about 5 mutually exclusive views of the same data on the same page (time range, layout, chart metric).
- Exceptions: For more than about 5 ranges, or custom ranges, use a select or date-range picker.
- Do: "24 hours | 7 days | 30 days" above a traffic chart, with the active segment marked as selected.
- Don't: A segmented control choosing the account's default currency.
- Check (static): Every segmented control is a role=tablist or a group of aria-pressed buttons with 2-5 items, and its handler only changes view state or the URL query, never calls a settings save endpoint.
- Check (live): Click each segment; the data view changes, no "saved" toast appears, and the network panel shows only read requests.

### CTL-009 — Every control has its own accessible name

**Rule:** Give every checkbox, switch, radio and select a unique accessible name taken from its visible label, and link its description programmatically.

- Why: Generic or repeated names ("Switch", the same label on every row, unnamed radios) make settings unusable with a screen reader and untestable by automation.
- Confidence: low (source inferred; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Always, for every form control.
- Exceptions: None.
- Do: Switch announced as "Always use HTTPS, switch, on", with its helper sentence read as description.
- Don't: Ten switches each announced as "Switch", or a radio group whose radios have no name.
- Check (static): Run an accessibility linter (axe rules label, aria-toggle-field-name, duplicate names within a page section); every input has a <label for>, aria-label or aria-labelledby, and helper text is wired with aria-describedby.
- Check (live): Dump the accessibility tree of each settings page; no checkbox, switch, radio or combobox has an empty, generic ("Switch", "Checkbox") or duplicated name.

### CTL-010 — On/off gates its dependent options

**Rule:** When a feature switch or checkbox controls further options, keep those options next to it and disable or reveal them according to its state.

- Why: Users see at a glance which options matter now, and cannot edit values that have no effect while the feature is off.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: A master on/off has 1 or more sub-options that only matter when it is on.
- Exceptions: Prefer disabled-but-visible when users need to know the options exist (for example to decide whether to turn the feature on); prefer hidden when the sub-form is long.
- Do: "Inspect traffic" switch off; the "Ports" radio group below it stays visible but disabled.
- Don't: Sub-options that stay editable while the feature they configure is off.
- Check (static): Each dependent control's disabled or hidden state is derived from its parent toggle's value, and it sits directly under that toggle in the same card.
- Check (live): Turn the parent off; dependent controls become disabled (aria-disabled or disabled) or hidden. Turn it on; they become editable without a reload.

## save-model

### SAV-001 — Sticky save bar that wakes on change

**Rule:** On a multi-field form, put Save and Discard in one sticky bar that stays disabled or hidden until the form has unsaved changes.

- Why: A Save control that is active only when something changed tells the user at a glance whether there is work to commit, and a sticky bar keeps it reachable on long pages.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: A page or object form holds several editable fields that are committed together.
- Exceptions: Independent sections on one page (see SAV-003); pages whose only controls apply at once (see SAV-002); read-only views (see SAV-007).
- Do: Bottom or top sticky bar with "Save" (primary) and "Discard" (secondary), both disabled while the form is clean; Save enables on the first edit.
- Don't: An always-enabled Save at the end of a long page that does nothing when clicked on an unchanged form.
- Check (static): In the form component, Save and Discard are disabled (or the bar is not rendered) when the dirty flag is false; the bar uses position sticky or fixed and lives outside the scrolling content.
- Check (live): Load the page; assert Save has the disabled attribute or the bar is absent. Change one field; assert Save becomes enabled and the bar is still visible after scrolling to the top and bottom. Revert the field to its original value; assert Save is disabled again.

### SAV-002 — Instant controls apply at once and confirm with a toast

**Rule:** Persist an instant control's change on toggle, confirm each change with a toast, and on failure revert the control and show an error with Retry. The choice of a switch for such settings, and the ban on switches in Save forms, is CTL-002.

- Why: Without a toast the user cannot tell whether an immediate change succeeded, and a control that stays flipped after a failed request shows a state the server does not have.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: A single on/off setting is independent of other fields and safe to apply without review.
- Exceptions: Options that must be reviewed together or have side effects use a checkbox inside an explicit-save form instead. If immediate apply is not wanted, do not use a switch.
- Do: Switch "Always use HTTPS" with no Save nearby; flipping it shows a toast "Setting updated" (error variant with Retry if the request fails) and reverts the switch on failure.
- Don't: A switch that flips silently, or stays on after the request failed.
- Check (static): Every switch change handler calls the API, emits a toast on success and on error, and restores the previous value on error.
- Check (live): Toggle each switch; assert a role=status or toast live region announces the result within 5 seconds and that reloading the page keeps the new state. Block the request in devtools and toggle again; the switch must return to its previous state with an error message.

### SAV-003 — Save per section when sections are independent

**Rule:** When a settings page holds sections that change different things, give each section its own Save (or a summary row that opens its own editor) instead of one page-wide Save.

- Why: Independent sections committed together force the user to save unrelated edits at once and make it unclear which change caused an error.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: A settings page groups unrelated settings into cards or sections, or a section is a single field such as a name or email.
- Exceptions: Fields that only make sense together stay in one form with one Save. Do not move a large form into a modal; open a subpage instead.
- Do: Card "Label format" ends with its own Save; settings row "Payments - Active >" opens a subpage or small dialog with its own Save; a single field "Account name" has an inline "Change name" button.
- Don't: One page-level Save that commits label format, pickup address and notification copy together.
- Check (static): Each card or section with editable fields owns exactly one commit action scoped to its fields; no page-level Save coexists with section Saves on the same page.
- Check (live): Edit a field in section A; assert only section A's Save enables. Save it; reload; assert section B is unchanged and section A persisted.

### SAV-004 — Discard returns to the last saved state

**Rule:** Pair every explicit Save with a Discard or Cancel that restores the last saved values, enabled only while there are unsaved changes.

- Why: Users explore settings; a one-click way back avoids retyping old values from memory.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any form or section with an explicit Save.
- Exceptions: Single-action buttons that commit at once (Print, Import, Purge) have no Discard.
- Do: "Discard changes" next to Save, disabled until an edit; optionally a confirm step when many fields changed.
- Don't: Only a browser Back button as the way to abandon edits.
- Check (static): The Discard handler resets the form to the last fetched server values, not to empty or to defaults; Discard shares Save's dirty-state enablement.
- Check (live): Change two fields; click Discard; assert both fields show their previous values and Save is disabled again. Reload; assert nothing was persisted.

### SAV-005 — Warn before leaving with unsaved changes

**Rule:** When the user navigates away from a form with unsaved changes, block the navigation and ask whether to leave and lose the changes.

- Why: Settings forms are long-lived; a silent navigation loses work and the user only notices later.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: A form with an explicit Save has a dirty state and the user clicks a nav link, Back, closes the tab or switches scope.
- Exceptions: Instant-apply pages and clean forms never prompt. Background jobs keep running and need no guard (see SAV-009).
- Do: Dialog "Leave page with unsaved changes? Your edits will be lost." with "Leave page" (critical) and "Stay".
- Don't: Navigating away silently, or prompting on every navigation even when nothing changed.
- Check (static): The router has a navigation guard and a beforeunload listener that are active only when the form's dirty flag is true.
- Check (live): Edit a field, click a sidebar link; assert a confirmation dialog appears and choosing Stay keeps the edit. Repeat with a clean form; assert navigation happens without a prompt.

### SAV-006 — Destructive actions stand apart and state the consequence

**Rule:** Put destructive actions in their own button, away from Save, with text that states the consequence, and confirm them in a dialog whose primary button names the action.

- Why: Mixing irreversible actions with routine saves invites misclicks; a dialog that says what will be lost lets the user make an informed choice.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Delete, remove, cancel subscription, purge, disconnect, or any bulk action that cannot be reversed or disrupts service.
- Exceptions: Removing an unsaved row inside a form being edited is part of that form's Discard and needs no dialog.
- Do: Section "Delete your profile" at the page end with "Permanently deletes this user"; dialog "Delete profile?" with critical "Delete profile" and "Cancel". A "Note:" line under Purge saying it may slow the site for a while.
- Don't: A red Delete next to Save in the same bar; a dialog with "Are you sure?" and "OK".
- Check (static): Destructive buttons use the critical variant, sit in a separate section or overflow menu, open a confirm dialog, and the dialog's primary label is a verb plus object (never Yes/OK/Confirm).
- Check (live): Click each destructive button; assert a dialog opens before any request is sent, its body states the consequence, and Escape or Cancel closes it with no change.

### SAV-007 — Read-only views carry no save controls

**Rule:** Do not render a Save bar or Save button on read-only tabs such as logs, history or reports.

- Why: A disabled Save on a page with nothing to edit makes users hunt for the editable field and erodes trust in the save signal.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: A tab or page shows only data or logs, even inside a settings area that otherwise has a save bar.
- Exceptions: none
- Do: Settings > Integrations has a save bar on the Settings tab and none on the Logs tab.
- Don't: A greyed-out Save bar under an import log table.
- Check (static): The save bar is rendered by the editable form component, not by the settings layout, so tabs without a form never include it.
- Check (live): Open every tab of each settings area; on tabs with no input, textbox, select, checkbox or switch, assert no button named Save exists.

### SAV-008 — Activity log records who changed what

**Rule:** Keep an account-level activity log of changes with time, actor (user, system or integration), action and, for settings, the old and new value, filterable and exportable.

- Why: Without undo, the log is how teams find out why something changed and restore the previous value; it also separates user edits from automated ones.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any dashboard where settings or shared objects can be changed by more than one person, an integration or the system.
- Exceptions: Purely personal preferences (theme, language) may be left out of the shared log.
- Do: Log row "2026-10-27 12:05 - Jane (web) - Default package weight changed from 0.5 kg to 1 kg"; filter by date, actor and action; Export. Object pages also show a timeline of their own events.
- Don't: A log that says only "Settings updated" with no field, value or actor.
- Check (static): Every settings mutation writes an audit record with timestamp, actor type and id, source interface, target, field, old value and new value; the log page has date and field filters.
- Check (live): Change one setting; open the activity log; assert a new row shows your user, the field name, the previous and the new value; filter by that field and by date and assert the row remains.

### SAV-009 — Long jobs run in the background and say so

**Rule:** For a commit that starts a long job, show a status line saying the job runs in the background, that the user can leave the page, and where to see progress.

- Why: Users otherwise wait on a spinner or abandon the page fearing the job will stop.
- Confidence: low (source observed; shopify absent, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: An action takes longer than a few seconds (catalogue rebuild, bulk import, export, migration).
- Exceptions: Short requests that finish before a toast would show.
- Do: "The catalogue runs in the background. You can leave this page and return to check progress." plus a progress indicator on return.
- Don't: A modal spinner that blocks the whole page until the job ends.
- Check (static): Long-running commits return a job id; the page renders job status from that id, not from an in-flight request.
- Check (live): Start the job; assert a status line says it runs in the background and the page can be left. Navigate away and back; assert no leave-page prompt appeared and the current progress is shown.

### SAV-011 — Assistant-proposed changes use the normal save path

**Rule:** When an AI assistant changes data, stage the change in the normal form or a confirmation card and apply it only after the user saves or approves.

- Why: The user keeps one mental model of when changes apply, and every AI change gets the same review, discard and audit trail as a manual one.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The dashboard has an assistant that can write settings or objects.
- Exceptions: Read-only assistant actions (search, explain, navigate) run without confirmation.
- Do: The assistant fills the price field and the save bar appears; or a card "Change SSL mode to Full - Approve / Decline" where Decline leaves everything unchanged.
- Don't: The assistant writes the setting directly and reports "Done" in chat.
- Check (static): Assistant write tools return a draft or patch applied to the form state or rendered as an approval card; no assistant tool calls a mutation endpoint without an approval step.
- Check (live): Ask the assistant to change a setting; assert nothing persists until Save or Approve is clicked; decline and reload; assert the value is unchanged and the audit log has no entry.

## microcopy

### MCP-001 — Buttons start with a verb and name the object

**Rule:** Label every action button with an imperative verb followed by the object it acts on, and keep a bare verb only when the object is unambiguous from the surrounding card or dialog.

- Why: A verb tells users the button does something, and the object tells them to what; a list of verb + object buttons can be scanned without reading the page around it.
- Confidence: medium (source documented; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Primary and secondary buttons on pages, cards, toolbars and dialogs.
- Exceptions: Standard short commands whose object is the whole form or dialog (Save, Cancel, Close, Export, Import) may stay a bare verb, as may Edit and Apply inside a card or dialog that names its object; toggles that show a state use the state or setting name instead.
- Do: "Add product", "Create rule", "Rotate token", "Print label".
- Don't: "New", "Add new", "OK", "Go", "Submit" on a page with several objects.
- Check (static): Extract all button labels from the component tree or string catalog; flag any whose first word is not a verb from the product's verb list, and any lone verb outside the allowed set (Save, Cancel, Close, Export, Import, Edit, Apply).
- Check (live): Dump the accessibility tree of each index and detail page; every role=button with visible text must start with a verb from the verb list, and the primary button of an index page must contain the singular of the H1 noun (H1 "Products", button "Add product") unless it is on the allowed bare-verb list.

### MCP-002 — Sentence case for all interface text

**Rule:** Write menu items, page titles, headings, tabs, column headers, buttons and section labels in sentence case, capitalising only the first word and proper names, and never store labels in ALL CAPS.

- Why: One casing rule removes a whole class of inconsistency; mixed Title Case and sentence case on one screen looks unfinished, and ALL CAPS text is slower to read and is spelled out letter by letter by some screen readers.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl observed, cloudflare documented)
- Applies when: All visible labels and headings in the product.
- Exceptions: Proper product or feature names and acronyms keep their own capitalisation (API, DNS). A small uppercase eyebrow style may be applied with CSS text-transform as long as the source string stays in sentence case.
- Do: "Shipping and delivery", "Edge certificates", "Create purchase order", column "Expires on".
- Don't: "Posture Findings" beside "Cloud & SaaS findings"; heading "Active Subscriptions"; a hard-coded "ORDER MANAGEMENT" string.
- Check (static): Lint the string catalog; flag strings with two or more capitalised words that are not in the proper-name allowlist, and strings that are entirely uppercase.
- Check (live): On each page, read element.textContent (the source string, before CSS text-transform) of every heading, tab, columnheader, button and nav link; report any label with two or more capitalised words not in the proper-name allowlist, and any label that is entirely uppercase in the source.

### MCP-003 — Destinations are nouns, commands are verbs

**Rule:** In every menu (sidebar, user menu, overflow menu), word items that open a page as nouns and items that perform an action as verbs, so the wording tells users what will happen on click.

- Why: Users predict the result of a click from its grammar; a noun promises a place, a verb promises a change, and mixing them misleads.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Sidebar navigation, tabs, user and account menus, overflow menus that mix links and actions.
- Exceptions: Overflow menus that only hold actions on one object are all verbs. A nav item for a single dominant task may use the task noun ("Search") rather than the verb.
- Do: Sidebar "Orders", "Pickups"; user menu "Profile", "Billing", "Log out".
- Don't: Sidebar "Manage users", "View reports"; user menu "Go to billing" next to "Profile".
- Check (static): In nav and menu definitions, flag items with an href whose label starts with a verb, and items with an onClick action (no href) whose label does not start with a verb.
- Check (live): Open each menu; for every menuitem or link, read whether it carries an href; items with an href must not start with a verb, items without an href must start with a verb from the verb list.

### MCP-004 — Short button labels without filler

**Rule:** Keep button labels to one to three words, verb first, with no articles, no "new", no "now" and no explanatory clause; put any explanation in helper text next to the button.

- Why: Short labels fit in toolbars and narrow screens and are read at a glance; filler words push the object out of view and make labels inconsistent.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: All buttons and menu commands.
- Exceptions: A qualifier is allowed when two buttons on the same screen would otherwise collide ("Create custom rule" next to "Create rate limiting rule").
- Do: "Add rule", "Test connection", "Import orders", "Add identity provider".
- Don't: "Add a new rule", "Run rules now", "Test to ensure it works", "Click here to import".
- Check (static): Flag button strings longer than three words unless listed as a collision qualifier, and strings containing the whole words "a", "an", "the", "new", "now", "here" or "please".
- Check (live): On each page, list button accessible names (visible text, not aria-label extensions added for MCP-005); report any over three words or containing the filler words above as whole words.

### MCP-005 — Repeated buttons name their object

**Rule:** When the same action appears on several rows or cards, include the object in the accessible name (visible or via aria-label) so each instance is unique.

- Why: A screen-reader or voice user who hears "Pin, Pin, Pin" or "Add new" ten times cannot tell which item each button affects; automation and tests cannot target them either.
- Confidence: low (source inferred; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Row actions in tables and lists, card actions repeated across a grid, per-item pin/star/remove buttons.
- Exceptions: The visible label may stay short ("Pin") if the accessible name adds the object ("Pin Invoices").
- Do: Visible "Remove", accessible name "Remove shipping method Standard"; "Sort by order date".
- Don't: Thirty buttons all named "Pin"; every card with an "Add new" button.
- Check (static): In list and table row templates, check that action buttons receive an aria-label or visually hidden text interpolating the row's name; lint for duplicate accessible names within one page.
- Check (live): Dump the accessibility tree per page; group buttons by accessible name; any name repeated more than once that is not a global control (Close, Save) is a failure.

### MCP-006 — One verb per kind of action

**Rule:** Define a product-wide verb list (for example "Add" to put an existing or simple item into a list, "Create" to build a new configured object, "Remove" to take out of a list, "Delete" to destroy) and use each verb only for its meaning.

- Why: When the same act is called "Add new", "Add a new rule" and "Create rule" on neighbouring pages, users wonder whether they are different operations; a fixed verb list makes behaviour predictable.
- Confidence: low (source inferred; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Any product with more than one create or remove flow.
- Exceptions: Domain verbs with a fixed meaning for the user (Print, Deploy, Rotate, Purge) are kept and added to the list rather than replaced by a generic verb.
- Do: Every list uses "Add <item>"; every configurable object uses "Create <object>"; Remove takes out of a list, Delete destroys.
- Don't: "Add new" on one rules page, "Create rule" on the next, "Delete" used for unlinking a member.
- Check (static): Keep the verb list in the string catalog or a lint config; grep button labels and flag verbs not on the list and the same object noun paired with two different create verbs.
- Check (live): Collect every create-type button across index pages; for each object noun, confirm only one verb is used.

### MCP-007 — One term per concept, one concept per term

**Rule:** Keep a glossary and use the same term for a concept in the menu, page title, breadcrumbs, buttons, notifications and shortcuts, matching singular and plural, and never reuse one term for two different concepts.

- Why: Different words for the same thing ("Quotes" in the menu, "Quote" as the title) and the same word for different things ("Notifications" for toasts and for a settings tab) make users doubt they are in the right place.
- Confidence: low (source inferred; shopify absent, dhl absent, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Every user-facing noun for an object, area or feature.
- Exceptions: After a rename, the old term may survive only as a search alias, never as a visible label.
- Do: Menu "Quotes", title "Quotes", breadcrumb "Quotes"; toasts announced as "Status messages", alert rules under "Notifications".
- Don't: Menu "Quotes", page title "Quote"; "Notifications" meaning both toasts and email alerts.
- Check (static): Maintain a glossary file; derive nav labels, page titles and shortcut labels from the same keys; flag string-catalog entries that use a glossary synonym or differ only by plural from the canonical term.
- Check (live): For each nav item, compare its label with the H1, breadcrumb and tab title of the target page; flag any mismatch, including singular vs plural; flag any accessible name used both for a landmark or live region and for a nav link or tab that leads to a different page.

### MCP-008 — One spelling variant across the product

**Rule:** Choose one English variant (for example American) for the whole interface and spell every word, including variants of the same word, in that variant only.

- Why: Mixed spellings ("fulfillment" next to "fulfilment") look careless, break search and filtering by text, and suggest the strings come from different products.
- Confidence: high (source documented; shopify documented, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: All source-language strings, before translation.
- Exceptions: Text copied from a third party (carrier service names, integration names) keeps its original spelling.
- Do: "Customize", "Colors", "Fulfillment" everywhere in an American English product.
- Don't: "Fulfillment" in the menu and "fulfilment" in the settings help.
- Check (static): Run a spell checker set to the chosen locale over the string catalog (for example cspell with en-US only) and fail on words from the other variant.
- Check (live): Extract page text from every page in a crawl and check it with the same locale dictionary; report pages containing other-variant spellings.

## settings

### SET-001 — Work in the menu, rare configuration in settings

**Rule:** Put the objects and jobs people touch every day in the main menu, and put rarely changed account-wide configuration behind a settings or account-admin entry that is separate from those work items.

- Why: Frequency decides placement: the menu is scanned many times a day, so every item that is used once a quarter costs attention on every visit.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: Any admin dashboard with both day-to-day work objects (orders, products, records) and account configuration (defaults, connections, billing).
- Exceptions: An urgent, instant on/off control that people reach for during an incident (for example an emergency protection mode or a maintenance mode) may sit on the object's overview page, with its full configuration still in settings.
- Do: Menu: Home, Orders, Products, Customers, Reports. Settings: Payments, Taxes, Shipping defaults, Users, Billing.
- Don't: A top-level menu item 'Tax rates' or 'Label format' next to 'Orders'.
- Check (static): List every top-level work item in the main menu (excluding the separated settings or account-admin group) and every settings page. Flag any work item whose page is mostly form controls for account-wide defaults, and any settings page that holds a queue or list of daily work records.
- Check (live): Open the main menu and click each top-level work item; each must land on a list, queue or overview of work, not on a configuration form. Open settings and confirm no page there is a daily work queue.

### SET-002 — Per-object configuration on the object

**Rule:** Put configuration that belongs to one object on that object's own page, as a section or a Settings tab, never in global settings.

- Why: People change an object's options while looking at the object; sending them to global settings breaks the task and hides which object the option belongs to.
- Confidence: high (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: A setting changes the behaviour or data of one record (one product, one shipment, one service, one integration).
- Exceptions: A default that applies to all new objects belongs in settings; the object page then shows the per-object value and may override it (see SET-011). Objects that are themselves configuration (integrations, connections, notification templates) may have their list and detail pages inside settings; their options still sit on each object's own detail page.
- Do: Product page with a status, package and custom fields section; a service detail page with tabs Overview, Metrics, Settings.
- Don't: Settings > Products > choose a product from a dropdown > edit its options.
- Check (static): For each settings page, check whether any field needs an object picker (a select or search listing individual records) before it can be edited. Each such field must move to that object's detail page.
- Check (live): Open one object's detail page and confirm its own options are editable there (inline section or Settings tab). Open every shared settings page (one not dedicated to a single object) and confirm none has a field that edits only this object.

### SET-003 — Sub-area settings inside the sub-area

**Rule:** When the product has distinct sub-products, channels or installed apps, give each its own Settings item inside its own navigation group, at the same position in every group, preferably last.

- Why: Settings that only make sense inside one sub-area are found faster next to what they control, and the global settings list stays short.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl absent, cloudflare observed)
- Applies when: The dashboard hosts several sub-products, channels or third-party apps, each with its own navigation group and its own settings.
- Exceptions: A single-product tool with one coherent job (for example a shipping tool with about 25 settings pages) may keep all settings in one central area grouped by lifecycle; one of the reference portals does this successfully. The global settings may still list installed apps and channels, linking into each one's own Settings.
- Do: Sidebar group 'Email' with items Campaigns, Templates, Email settings; global settings only lists 'Apps and channels'.
- Don't: Global settings with 40 entries, half of them named after individual apps or sub-products.
- Check (static): For each sub-product or app navigation group, check that it contains one item labelled 'Settings' or '<Name> settings', at the same position in every group. Check that global settings holds no page specific to only one sub-product.
- Check (live): Open each sub-product group in the sidebar and confirm it has a settings item in the same position as in the other groups, and that it opens a page scoped to that sub-product. Open global settings and confirm it contains no sub-product-only options.

### SET-004 — Settings as a mode with its own navigation

**Rule:** When the user enters settings, show a dedicated settings navigation that replaces or sits beside the main menu, with a labelled link back to the main menu, and give every settings page its own URL.

- Why: A dedicated list keeps all settings pages one click apart and tells the user they are configuring, not working; the back link and real URLs prevent dead ends and allow sharing and bookmarking a page.
- Confidence: medium (source observed; shopify observed, dhl observed, cloudflare absent)
- Applies when: Settings span more than one page.
- Exceptions: A short settings area of one page with tabs needs no separate navigation, but each tab should still change the URL; one reference portal has no settings mode and uses tabs without URL changes for account configuration, which blocks deep links.
